question:
A compound microscope is used only as a light-collecting optical system (its focal lengths are not needed). At the plane just before the eyepiece, the light that will enter the eye (or detector) consists of two components:

1) **Signal (desired)**: diffuse light from a faint mark, **unpolarized**, of intensity $I_d$.
2) **Background (glare)**: specular reflection from the glossy surface, **completely linearly polarized**, of intensity $I_g=9I_d$.

Assume the microscope optics between the entrance pupil and this plane attenuate both components by the same factor and do **not** change their polarization states, so the above intensities and polarization descriptions apply at the analyzer plane.

An ideal analyzer is placed at this plane. Its transmission axis makes an angle $\theta$ with the polarization direction of the glare.

The transmitted light is then incident normally on a photoelectric detector of work function $\phi=2.0\,\text{eV}$ using monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda=400\,\text{nm}$. The anode is kept sufficiently positive (saturation conditions). Assume the saturation photocurrent is proportional to the total light intensity incident on the detector.

(i) Find the analyzer angle $\theta$ that maximizes the signal-to-background ratio $\dfrac{I_{\text{signal}}}{I_{\text{background}}}$ at the detector.

(ii) At this $\theta$, find the ratio of saturation photocurrents $\dfrac{I_s}{I_{s0}}$, where $I_{s0}$ is the saturation photocurrent when the analyzer is absent.

(iii) Find the stopping potential $V_s$ of the detector.

Use $hc=1240\,\text{eV}\cdot\text{nm}$.
